blocks.p: Stillness is a mixed state. When two (or all) primary states are active simultaneously, they create a mixed state. If you mix two primary colors, you get a secondary color, right? Red paint mixed with blue paint makes purple paint. Same with Polyvagal primary states.
Safety + Shutdown = Stillness
Safety + Shutdown + x = Intimacy
Stillness and intimacy are basically the same mixed state with one significant difference. I'll discuss stillness first, then intimacy.

Stillness is a combination of shutdown plus safety. Stillness is the ability to immobilize in safety, to not move, and to be okay with it. It is calm, relaxed, and reflective. It allows someone to sit silently, use the restroom, or lie down and fall asleep.

Individuals in a defensive state have difficulty with immobilization. Someone in flight/fight may experience danger when immobile. For them, immobility is unsafe: they've exposed themselves to danger by immobilizing. Their body would be primed to run or fight if they were in the wild. They wouldn't sit down while mobilized for flight/fight. The gazelle running from a lion doesn't lie down to go to sleep. They use the energy within them. Stillness, safe immobility, is not an option.

The immobility of stillness is without fear. Immobility with fear is freeze. In freeze, the immobilization is sympathetically charged, which is felt as fear. The immobility of stillness also lacks the dysregulation of shutdown. If shutdown is dominant, then stillness is inaccessible. Instead, the individual feels hopeless, helpless, empty, and numb. That's shutdown immobilization, but not stillness.

Children in a sympathetic state will find sitting in a classroom environment challenging. First, just being immobile is a tall order. That child is ready to run or fight, not sit. But the environment and situation itself will also have numerous danger cues keeping the child down their ladder: people, sounds, pressure, falling behind in class, feeling dumb, teacher comments/sarcasm, and more.

Traumatized individuals often have difficulty with things like meditation or yoga for the same reasons. They're immobilized and now open to "danger." Closing their eyes during meditation is another potential danger. Certain poses may trigger a neuroception of danger in yoga based on that person's history.

Compounding the issue is what the person finds when looking inward. Activities like meditation and yoga involve and require a lot of self-reflection and awareness somatically, emotionally, and cognitively. When immobilized and focused inward, there's no filter between awareness and what one may otherwise avoid that is still alive within them. Those memories, thoughts, and feelings will be felt in these moments of unsafe immobility. And on top of all that is the potential vulnerability of being around others.

Another experience of potentially unsafe immobility is sleep. Or, more likely, lying awake before falling asleep. Lying down to sleep, in the dark, with your eyes closed, in the silence of night is filled with danger cues. And maybe even worse if the person next to you is a danger cue as well or a past traumatic incident involved any of these potentially triggering pieces already listed.

Lying down and immobilizing to go to sleep potentially brings a lot of stress, anxiety, and worry, especially for the person who spends more time in flight/fight or freeze. In this context, your sympathetic state is active, and distracting yourself is now removed as a coping option. You're just... lying there. Immobilized. While possibly charged to run or fight or living with fear in your system. Thoughts shift along with your state and your feelings. Anxious thoughts like what needs to be accomplished the next day, something you didn't do that day, memories of the past, and panic about not falling asleep might fill your head.

Like mobilization, anything is unsafe without an active social engagement system. If you're immobile, that means being open to a predator. That's the message your body will send to your brain. Your brain needs the social engagement system active to handle the immobilization and repurpose it for stillness.

Unfortunately, we need stillness throughout the day to get through a class, work, sleep, and use the restroom. These and other instances aren't exactly something we can escape either. We're stuck. Our bodies are charged if we exist down the ladder in flight/fight, but then we're immobilized throughout the day with no option of fighting or running. So our bodies don't get the relief of energy discharge. It just stays within us.
So we adapt. We do things to deal with the immobilization necessary in stillness. Not solve the problem. Just deal with it.

While you're lying down to go to sleep, do you have a screen on? Something to distract you while you lay there? Something to listen to, like music? Or a white noise machine? Do you drink or get high? These are ways to distract ourselves from what's happening within. They are external ways of coping with the internal world. They are ways to get enough relief from our distress that we can immobilize and maybe even fall asleep.

In the classroom, children often create behavior problems to avoid the unsafe feelings of immobilization. Behavior problems bring a sense of danger, which matches their internal state and provides the danger they are constantly scanning for. They may also be an outlet in and of themselves: a way to use flight/fight energy by fighting with a peer or running from one, for example.

The problem is that it doesn't actually solve anything. The energy isn't actually released. It's probably reinforced because the student is again in a situation where they are perceiving danger without a way to discharge the energy efficiently. These behavior problems create further problems, like getting in trouble, being shamed, and missing out on valuable social time. Students like this might be better served with classroom mindfulness strategies combined with fidgets: a way to immobilize and have an outlet for their flight/fight activation.

blocks.why: Stillness is built a few safe minutes at a time. This practice is one of those few minutes, with your eyes open if you like.

blocks.p: Intimacy, like stillness, involves the ventral vagal safety pathways active along with the dorsal vagal shutdown pathways: safe but immobile. However, it also involves the addition of one key variable: intimacy requires someone else to be present. The two individuals offer each other safety cues, just like with play. Intimacy can then be understood as stillness with a safe other.

blocks.prompt: Name one instance from this past week when you felt your stillness mixed state active. How do you know it was stillness?
When was the last time you felt calm, relaxed, okay with being still, and connected to the present moment through your senses?
Can you identify any ways that you have of coping with immobility?

q: "In reptiles, due their limited need for oxygen, immobilization is a very effective defense strategy. In contrast, since mammals have a great need for oxygen, the inhibition of movement coupled with a shift in autonomic state to support the immobilization behavior (i.e., apnea and bradycardia) can be lethal. However, several aspects of mammalian social behavior require immobilization, but immobilization without fear." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2003). Social engagement and attachment: A phylogenetic perspective. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1008, 31–47. [doi.org/10.1196/annals.1301.004](https://doi.org/10.1196/annals.1301.004)

blocks.p: My translation: Reptiles can immobilize in defense with no problem. Mammals don't do well with this defensive strategy because we need more oxygen. We also need to immobilize without fear for social behaviors, like caring for newborns.

q: "The 'good' immobilization response, immobilization without fear, requires the co-opting of the neural pathways involved in 'immobilization with fear' with neuropeptides, such as oxytocin. Functionally oxytocin has receptors in the brainstem dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus that regulates the phylogenetically older unmyelinated vagus. This system of immobilization without fear enables women to give birth without fainting or dying. The same 'good' immobilization system enables people to cuddle and hug without problems and enables women to breast-feed without having to move." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Prengel, S. (2011). Conversation with Stephen Porges. Somatic Perspectives on Psychotherapy. [polyvagalinstitute.org](https://www.polyvagalinstitute.org/_files/ugd/5504d5_28468bfb53314717b1a5e6ea567af716.pdf)

blocks.p: My translation: Oxytocin allows us to immobilize without fear and also connect with each other.
